sentences.text: Mauriciosaurus is a genus of polycotylid plesiosaur, a group of marine reptiles, that lived in Mexico during the Late Cretaceous. This animal possessed a drop-shaped body, a short neck, and a small tail.

It is morphologically most similar to the polycotylids Trinacromerum and Dolichorhynchops. Distinctive features include a complex ridge pattern on the parasphenoid, narrow palate openings, a lack of coracoid perforations, and a unique arrangement of belly ribs similar to Cryptoclidus.
Each side of the upper jaw contained at least 42 teeth, comprising 4 in the premaxilla and 32 in the maxilla.

Mauriciosaurus was described in 2017 based on a single well-preserved juvenile specimen approximately 2 meters long. The only known specimen was discovered in the summer of 2011 by workers at a quarry near Vallecillo in Nuevo León, Mexico.

The fossil material consists of 28 slabs from the Agua Nueva Formation in the municipality of Vallecillo, Nuevo León. The only known specimen belongs to the private collection of Mexican politician Mauricio Fernández Garza, and a replica is displayed at the Papalote Museo del Niño in Monterrey.

The animal possessed flexible trailing edges on its flippers that acted as hydrofoils and a body outline shaped by contour fat merging the torso and tail. Adult individuals of Mauriciosaurus would have reached up to twice the length of the juvenile type specimen.

Researchers interpret preserved soft tissue in Mauriciosaurus as a peritoneum richly pigmented by melanocytes. A heavily pigmented lining protected the animal's internal organs from UV exposure. In modern desert or high-altitude squamates, peritoneal pigmentation protects reproductive organs from solar ultraviolet radiation, a function hypothesized for Mauriciosaurus.
Mauriciosaurus likely hunted small prey because it had a slender snout and small, pointed teeth.

Mauriciosaurus was assigned to the family Polycotylidae by Frey et al. in 2017. Mauriciosaurus is classified within the subfamily Polycotylinae based on characteristics such as the length-to-width ratio of the humerus.
Frey et al. diagnosed Mauriciosaurus as a new genus based on narrow interpterygoid vacuities, lack of coracoid perforations, and a specialized gastralia arrangement.

The presence of the ammonite Mammites nodosoides allows the specimen to be dated to the Turonian interval. Biostratigraphic analysis dates the slab containing Mauriciosaurus to the early Turonian portion of the Agua Nueva Formation.
The habitat was the bottom of a continental shelf approximately 500 km offshore in the prehistoric Gulf of Mexico.
Several unique features separate Mauriciosaurus from all other polycotylids, justifying its classification as a distinct genus.
